channel.title: BrainiLab Learn
channel.description: Curious questions, clear answers and games to try.

item.title: Could you draw a familiar logo from memory?
item.description: A logo can feel familiar while its details stay fuzzy. Try a quick drawing challenge, then discover what an Apple-logo study found about confidence and memory.

item.title: What does adding actually mean?
item.description: Put two little piles together and count what you have. Try moving counters, learn what + and = mean, and build your first sums.

item.title: Multiplication starts with equal groups
item.description: A few bowls of fruit can explain multiplication. Build equal groups, count them, and explore a times table without memorising it first.

item.title: Subtraction: what is left when you take some away?
item.description: Start with a small pile, take a few away, and count what remains. Try it yourself, then use addition to check your answer.

item.title: Can a wrong guess help you learn the answer?
item.description: Guessing before reading can sometimes help you learn. Try a short question, then see what a pretesting study found—and what it did not.

item.title: How did a burr inspire a fastener you can pull apart?
item.description: A plant burr clinging to fabric gave George de Mestral an idea. Look closely at the hooks and loops behind a familiar reusable fastener.

item.title: Why is there a tiny ball in a ballpoint pen?
item.description: A ballpoint pen does more than let ink out of a tube. Its rolling tip transfers ink to the page—and helped solve a problem with thicker ink.

item.title: Why did Britain skip 11 days in 1752?
item.description: Go to bed on 2 September. Wake up on 14 September. That happened in Britain in 1752—but nobody slept for eleven extra nights.

item.title: Why did tennis balls turn yellow?
item.description: Tennis balls were not always yellow. Television helped change their colour, but Wimbledon kept its white balls for another fourteen years.

item.title: How can a word mean its own opposite?
item.description: Dust can mean adding something or taking it away. Meet contronyms, the words that pull in two directions, and try a few examples.

item.title: Two Ls, two different colours: how repeated letters work
item.description: One L turns yellow; the other turns grey. A worked example explains what repeated letters tell you in a five-letter word puzzle.

item.title: How a slipping bookmark helped invent Post-it Notes
item.description: A bookmark that kept falling out gave an unusual adhesive a purpose. Meet the two inventors behind Post-it Notes and the problem they solved.

item.title: Was bubble wrap really invented as wallpaper?
item.description: Before it protected parcels, bubble wrap was meant to decorate walls. The familiar packing material began with a very different plan.

item.title: 5 number puzzles for a coffee break — free printable
item.description: A pencil, four numbers and a target. Try five original Number Route puzzles online or print the two-page sheet with explained answers.

item.title: An easier way to add numbers in your head
item.description: Start with a handful of counters, then try 38 + 27. One small change can make a sum easier, as long as you undo it afterwards.

item.title: How to play Number Route: follow the running total
item.description: Four numbers, three missing signs and one target. Learn the left-to-right rule with a complete example, then try a route yourself.

item.title: What do the Olympic rings and their colours mean?
item.description: Five rings, five colours and one common misconception. Here’s the story behind the Olympic symbol.

item.title: Multiplying by 11: ten groups, then one more
item.description: Picture eleven bags with the same number of sweets in each. Count ten bags first, then add the last one. We’ll take it one step at a time.

item.title: Stalactites and stalagmites: what’s the difference?
item.description: One hangs from the ceiling; the other grows from the floor. Here’s how to tell them apart and remember their names.

item.title: Why will 2100 skip its leap day?
item.description: Most of us learn that a leap year comes every four years. There is a small extra rule, and the year 2100 is where it matters.

item.title: How tennis scoring works, from love to deuce
item.description: What does 30–40 mean, and what happens at deuce? Follow the points through a game, a set and a tie-break.

item.title: Why is Canberra Australia’s capital?
item.description: Sydney and Melbourne were rivals for the role. The solution was a new capital, with a location written into the Constitution.

item.title: How to find the link in a Connections puzzle
item.description: A word can have more than one meaning. Here’s how to spot the connection that fits every clue.

item.title: Why does thunder come after lightning?
item.description: The delay between a flash and its thunder tells you how far the sound has travelled. Here’s how the estimate works.

item.title: How to read Roman numerals
item.description: Learn the seven symbols, spot the subtraction pairs and turn a date such as MCMXLIV into a number you recognise.

item.title: What does a percentage mean? Start with 100 squares
item.description: Percentages are a way to describe a part of something. Start with shaded squares, then use halves and small equal groups to make sense of the numbers.

item.title: How to spot patterns in number sequences
item.description: Look at the gaps, try multiplication and check alternate terms. Four approaches to finding what comes next.

item.title: How to remember what you learn in a quiz
item.description: An answer can feel obvious as soon as you see it. Try recalling it later, without the clues, to see what has stuck.

item.title: Why is summer warmer than winter?
item.description: Earth leans as it travels around the Sun. That small tilt changes how much sunlight reaches us—and how long it stays light each day.

item.title: Which century is a year in? Think of boxes of 100
item.description: A century is a group of one hundred years. Imagine putting the years into numbered boxes and the awkward dates start to make sense.

item.title: Why does Greenland look so big on a map?
item.description: On a Mercator map, places near the poles look larger than they really are relative to the rest of the world. Here’s why.

item.title: Why do octopuses have three hearts?
item.description: Two hearts send blood to the gills, while a third supplies the body. And that blood has an unusual colour.

item.title: Why does the Moon seem to change shape?
item.description: One night it looks like a thin smile; another night it is a bright circle. The Moon stays round. What changes is how much of its sunlit side we can see.

item.title: Why isn’t it the same time everywhere?
item.description: Your afternoon might be someone else’s morning. Start with a turning Earth, then see why the lines on a time-zone map bend around countries.

item.title: Daily or Anytime: what would you like to play?
item.description: Take on today’s shared challenges or choose a quiz on a favourite topic. A quick guide to finding your next game.

item.title: How to learn world flags without mixing them up
item.description: Start with a few flags, notice their distinctive details and compare the pairs that keep catching you out.
